counterevidenceSearch: Directed searches and findings: (1) Riegel conversion in recreational runners: well calibrated up to the half marathon but marathon times underestimated by 10 min or more for about half of runners, with a 5th-centile residual of -36 min (SRC01); individual exponents of club runners centre near 1.12, above the 1.06 world-record value (SRC02); no single marathon equation is accurate across abilities, SEE up to 27.4 min (SRC04); slower runners race less consistently (SRC03, SRC05). This changed the proposed exponents, restricted the marathon estimate and widened the margins. (2) Pace or zone derivation from a single performance or a fixed fraction: fixed percentages of maximal values place individuals in different intensity domains (SRC08, SRC09); this is why the fraction-based easy bands are ceilings subordinate to effort and are never called domains. (3) Field tests in novices: no direct trial of 3 km or 5 km field-test safety in novice runners was found; the ruling rests on the ACSM screening model (risk modulated by current activity, symptoms and intended intensity, SRC17), on low but non-zero race cardiac-arrest incidence (SRC18) and on pacing needing experience (SRC20). This is why P3 requires prior executed harder work and a non-maximal cue, and no test is offered to beginners. (4) Perceived-exertion anchors: the talk test tracks the ventilatory threshold with errors biased toward passing above it (SRC22); the existing cues therefore stay the prescription, and pace only constrains easy running from above. (5) HR maximum: age equations have poor individual agreement (SRC10, SRC11) and optical wrist sensors are less accurate than chest straps (SRC12). The null result for direct novice field-test safety evidence is logged as a search result, not proof that risk is absent.

sources.citation: Vickers AJ, Vertosick EA. An empirical study of race times in recreational endurance runners. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil 2016;8:26.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (Riegel k = 1.07, sensitivity analyses); Results (calibration up to half marathon); Table 4 (residual centiles); Discussion; limitations
sources.findingsUsed: 2,303 recreational runners (median age 35, 39% women, median marathon 3:54). Riegel with k = 1.07 was well calibrated up to the half marathon but dramatically underestimated marathon time: 10 min or more too fast for about half of runners, nearly 25% more than 20 min too fast; residual centiles 5th -36:17, 50th -10:09, 95th +5:12. Adding typical weekly mileage reduced error. Riegel cited k of 1.05-1.06 for male recreational runners aged 40-70.
limitations: prior race distance chosen as longest non-target race
few runners slower than about 6:30/km in the inter-quartile ranges

sources.citation: Blythe DA, Kiraly FJ. Prediction and quantification of individual athletic performance of runners. PLoS One 2016;11(6):e0157257.
sources.locator: Introduction (Riegel 1.06); Results (individual exponent median and percentiles; relation to performance and age); caveats
sources.findingsUsed: 164,746 British club runners: an individual power law fits well; individual exponents are higher than Riegel's world-record exponent (median 1.12; 5th-95th percentiles 1.10-1.15); a low exponent correlates with better performance; the exponent rises with age after about 20.
limitations: exponent fitted over 800 m upward, not only 5 km to marathon
authors caution against interpretation without validation

sources.citation: Emig T, Peltonen J. Human running performance from real-world big data. Nat Commun 2020;11:4936.
sources.locator: Results on marathon prediction error versus finishing time; limitations
sources.findingsUsed: About 14,000 tracker users: faster runners race more consistently across distances than slower runners; in the fastest group (marathon under 160 min) prediction error was typically under 2.5%; error grows with slower marathon times. Endurance (decline of sustainable power with duration) varies between individuals.
limitations: tracker data with total distance and duration only

sources.citation: Keogh A, Smyth B, Caulfield B, Lawlor A, Berndsen J, Doherty C. Prediction equations for marathon performance: a systematic review. Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2019;14(9):1159-1169.
sources.findingsUsed: 36 studies, 114 equations; r2 0.10-0.99, SEE 0.27-27.4 min; heterogeneity precludes a single best equation; gradient, sex and weather often missing; runners should not rely on a single equation.

sources.citation: Hopkins WG, Hewson DJ. Variability of competitive performance of distance runners. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2001;33(9):1588-92.
sources.findingsUsed: Within-athlete CV of official race times: 1.2-1.9% for the fastest male quartile in cross-country and road runs, 2.7% and 4.2% in half marathons, 2.6% in marathons; slower runners more variable (slower/faster CV ratio 1.0-2.3); younger adults more variable.

sources.citation: Smyth B, Muniz-Pumares D. Calculation of critical speed from raw training data in recreational marathon runners. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2020;52(12):2637-2645.
sources.findingsUsed: More than 25,000 recreational marathoners: CS from training data correlated with marathon performance (error about 8%); runners completed the marathon at 84.8% +/- 13.6% of CS, 93.0% for 150-min and 78.9% for 360-min finishers; a first half above 94% of CS was associated with marked second-half slowdown.

sources.citation: Jones AM, Burnley M, Black MI, Poole DC, Vanhatalo A. The maximal metabolic steady state: redefining the 'gold standard'. Physiol Rep 2019;7(10):e14098.
sources.findingsUsed: Exercise at critical power or speed is sustainable for no more than about 20-30 min; MLSS usually lies somewhat below it; CS bounds the heavy and severe domains; MLSS and CS are not synonymous.

sources.citation: Mann T, Lamberts RP, Lambert MI. Methods of prescribing relative exercise intensity: physiological and practical considerations. Sports Med 2013;43(7):613-25.
sources.findingsUsed: Exercise at a fixed %VO2max or %HRmax produces inter-individual variation in metabolic stress; some individuals are above and others below metabolic thresholds at the same percentage; threshold-anchored prescription expected to reduce variation.

sources.citation: Iannetta D, Inglis EC, Mattu AT, et al. A critical evaluation of current methods for exercise prescription in women and men. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2020;52(2):466-473.
sources.findingsUsed: 100 adults (46 women): LT and MLSS occurred at different %VO2max and %HRmax in women and men; fixed-percentage prescription conforms poorly to intensity domains.
limitations: abstract only; results sentence truncated in the record

sources.citation: Tanaka H, Monahan KD, Seals DR. Age-predicted maximal heart rate revisited. J Am Coll Cardiol 2001;37(1):153-6.
sources.findingsUsed: Group equation 208 - 0.7 x age from 351 studies and a 514-subject laboratory study; a population regression, not an individual measurement.
limitations: individual prediction error not in the abstract

sources.citation: Shookster D, Lindsey B, Cortes N, Martin JR. Accuracy of commonly used age-predicted maximal heart rate equations. Int J Exerc Sci 2020;13(7):1242-1250.
sources.findingsUsed: 99 maximal treadmill tests: all eight age-predicted equations showed poor agreement with measured HRmax, with proportional bias; measured HRmax recommended where applicable.

sources.citation: Gillinov S, Etiwy M, Wang R, et al. Variable accuracy of wearable heart rate monitors during aerobic exercise. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2017;49(8):1697-1703.
sources.findingsUsed: 50 adults: the chest-strap monitor agreed best with ECG (rc 0.996); optical wrist and forearm devices were less accurate (rc 0.67-0.92) and varied by exercise type.

sources.citation: Gilgen-Ammann R, Schweizer T, Wyss T. Accuracy of distance recordings in eight positioning-enabled sport watches: instrument validation study. JMIR Mhealth Uhealth 2020;8(6):e17118.
sources.findingsUsed: Mean absolute percentage distance errors of 3.2% to 6.1% across urban, forest and track settings for 404-4,297 m references; distances may be underestimated by up to 9%; best in open areas.

sources.citation: Jones AM, Doust JH. A 1% treadmill grade most accurately reflects the energetic cost of outdoor running. J Sports Sci 1996;14(4):321-7.
sources.findingsUsed: Treadmill running lacks air resistance and has a lower energy cost than outdoor running at the same speed; a small incline is needed to match it.

sources.citation: Mujika I, Padilla S. Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part I: short term insufficient training stimulus. Sports Med 2000;30(2):79-87.
sources.findingsUsed: Under 4 weeks of insufficient stimulus: rapid VO2max and blood-volume decline in highly trained athletes; endurance performance impaired; more moderate changes in recently trained individuals.

sources.citation: Mujika I, Padilla S. Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. Part II: long term insufficient training stimulus. Sports Med 2000;30(3):145-54.
sources.findingsUsed: Beyond 4 weeks: recently acquired VO2max gains are completely lost and endurance performance is impaired; reduced-training strategies that keep intensity limit losses.

sources.citation: Riebe D, Franklin BA, Thompson PD, et al. Updating ACSM's recommendations for exercise preparticipation health screening. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2015;47(11):2473-9.
sources.findingsUsed: Screening based on current physical activity, signs or symptoms or known disease, and desired intensity; exercise-related cardiovascular events are often preceded by warning signs; risk lessens as people become more active and fit.
limitations: cardiovascular screening model, not a field-test protocol

sources.citation: Kim JH, Rim AJ, Miller JT, et al. Cardiac arrest during long-distance running races. JAMA 2025;333(19):1699-1707.
sources.findingsUsed: US marathons and half marathons 2010-2023: cardiac arrest 0.54 per 100,000 participants; higher in men and in the marathon (1.04) than the half (0.47); coronary artery disease the most common determined cause.

sources.citation: Stevens CJ, Hacene J, Sculley DV, et al. The reliability of running performance in a 5 km time trial on a non-motorized treadmill. Int J Sports Med 2015;36(9):705-9.
sources.findingsUsed: 17 male runners, after familiarisation: 5 km time-trial CV 1.2%, ICC 0.99.

sources.citation: Mauger AR, Jones AM, Williams CA. Influence of feedback and prior experience on pacing during a 4-km cycle time trial. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2009;41(2):451-8.
sources.findingsUsed: Pacing in a time trial improves with prior experience and distance knowledge; the first trial without them was slower.

sources.citation: Reed JL, Pipe AL. The talk test: a useful tool for prescribing and monitoring exercise intensity. Curr Opin Cardiol 2014;29(5):475-80.
sources.findingsUsed: Comfortable speech is likely possible below the ventilatory or lactate threshold and not likely above it; consistent across modes including walking and jogging.

sources.citation: Foster C, Porcari JP, Anderson J, et al. The talk test as a marker of exercise training intensity. J Cardiopulm Rehabil Prev 2008;28(1):24-30.
sources.findingsUsed: The last positive talk-test stage tracked changes in the ventilatory threshold after training and blood donation; predictive errors were biased toward passing the test above VT.

sources.citation: Seiler KS, Kjerland GO. Quantifying training intensity distribution in elite endurance athletes: is there evidence for an 'optimal' distribution? Scand J Med Sci Sports 2006;16(1):49-56.
sources.findingsUsed: Three-zone intensity distribution was similar whether quantified by HR (zones from individually measured VT1/VT2) or session RPE.
limitations: zones from measured thresholds, not fractions

sources.citation: Munoz I, Seiler S, Bautista J, et al. Does polarized training improve performance in recreational runners? Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2014;9(2):265-72.
sources.findingsUsed: 30 recreational runners over 10 weeks with HR zones from measured VT and RCT: both programmes improved 10 km time; more low-intensity distribution gave larger effects.
limitations: abstract only; numeric results partly truncated
used only as context for magnitudes and low-intensity emphasis

sources.citation: Meeusen R, Duclos M, Foster C, et al. Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: joint consensus statement of the ECSS and ACSM. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2013;45(1):186-205.
sources.findingsUsed: Short-term performance decrement without lasting symptoms is functional overreaching; NFOR and OTS are hard to distinguish and need exclusion of organic disease or infection; no marker meets all criteria for general use.

globalConditions.condition: The planner is unchanged: sessions, durations, ladders, gates, phases, taper, race day and every safety rule stay byte for byte. With every boundary off, every output is byte-identical to 981a8f6. A band, zone or estimate never changes a dose, a gate, a progression, a race-day mode or an eligibility result.

The existing effort cue remains the prescription of every run. Pace bands and heart-rate zones are guidance beside it; when they disagree with the cue, the cue wins and the athlete slows. Missing pace or heart rate never blocks or degrades an effort-based prescription.

Kept standing rules: no pace from a goal time; nothing harder derived from easy pace; no text claims VO2max, LT1, LT2, MLSS, critical speed or lactate threshold; bands are named only by the engine's effort domains and labelled estimated or observed.

Calibration is a pure function of the record (intake facts, logged sessions, declared evidence) and changes only at a week boundary: the calibration of week w reads only evidence dated before week w starts. Every output carries its basis, the evidence id and date, the method, the confidence and, when absent, a typed unavailable reason.

During a clinical hold nothing is prescribed, so no band, zone or estimate is shown. Any symptom reported during an assessment or a run routes to the existing warning-sign screen and clinical route; this record sets no clinical route.
Effort domains, pace bands and heart-rate zones are three separate outputs; none is converted into another, and measured anchors are never equated with estimated ones.
Population: nonclinical recreational adults as in the R6 policy, running on roads or tracks. Trail, ultra and walk-run racing are outside the model (no band, no estimate).
Every athlete-facing text needs Product copy review before use; the disclosures below state required content, not final wording.

conditions: The kind is stored and shown with every output that uses it; a derived value is always labelled estimated; a presumed capacity is labelled presumed.
TRAINING_OBSERVATION feeds only P1, P2 and Q8; LAB_TEST feeds only Q6(a).
NONE gives effort-only guidance with a typed reason, never an error and never a penalty.
items.rationale: Separating historical, current, derived and presumed capacity is the precondition for honesty; prediction accuracy depends on recency and training (SRC01) and capacity decays with insufficient training (SRC15, SRC16).
items.disclosure: Each output names what it rests on: 'estimated from your 10 km race of <date>' or 'observed in your easy runs', never a bare number.

value.datedWithinCurrentWindow: read as the RACE_RESULT or TIME_TRIAL it is, with its measurement

conditions: An old best is never current capacity and is never shown as an estimate.
items.rationale: Detraining and training change capacity within weeks; a best without a date cannot be placed in time.
items.disclosure: A best is shown only as 'your best, <date>', separate from any estimate.

conditions: A result run with walk breaks, on trail, on a hilly course or in heat flagged by the athlete does not qualify as capacity evidence (it stays in the record as a result).
Tolerated means the athlete reports completing it without a warning sign; a reported symptom routes to the existing screen.
items.rationale: Course gradient and weather are major unmodelled error sources (SRC04); the model was examined on road races (SRC01).
items.disclosure: 'This result was run in conditions we cannot compare, so it is kept but not used for your paces.'

conditions: Changed from the proposal: GPS is one tier down (not equal to OFFICIAL), MANUAL and TREADMILL two tiers down (not one). OFFICIAL means official timing on a measured race course.
items.rationale: GPS distance errors of 3.2-6.1% (SRC13) exceed the HIGH margin; treadmill running differs in energy cost (SRC14) and belt calibration is unknown.
items.disclosure: The confidence label states the measurement: 'measured by GPS: moderate confidence'.

value.countedFrom: the first day of the week being calibrated

conditions: Changed from the proposal: AGING ends at 112 days (16 weeks, one program horizon), not 182.
items.rationale: Endurance capacity changes within weeks of altered training; a presumption beyond one program horizon is not defensible as current. The exact cut-offs are bounded choices, not physiological constants.
items.disclosure: A presumed reference reads 'presumed from a result <n> weeks old; low confidence'.

conditions: Applies to every capacity kind, races included. Added: an unknown effort report is also one tier down (it cannot be read as a hard effort).
items.rationale: A result run below a hard effort under-states capacity; using it as a lower bound is conservative but less informative.
items.disclosure: 'You reported this as moderate, so it is read as at least your current level.'

conditions: Tier = HIGH minus the summed reductions (measurement, effort, conflict, a 7-13 day break); AGING caps at LOW; three or more reductions make the capacity unavailable.
items.rationale: Additive, inspectable reductions keep confidence traceable to named causes.
items.disclosure: Confidence is shown as a word with its causes, never a score.

conditions: Comparison basis: the 10K-equivalent central time on the STANDARD model; a marathon result is compared only with another marathon result.

Within 28 days and more than 3% apart: the slower is the reference, one tier down, both flagged CONFLICTING_EVIDENCE. Within 3%: the most recent is the reference. A result more than 28 days older than the reference is superseded.
The fastest result is never chosen because it is fastest.
items.rationale: Race-to-race variation of 1.2-4.2%, larger in slower runners (SRC05), makes 3% roughly the edge of ordinary noise; beyond it, choosing the slower protects against an unrepresentative fast day or a short course.
items.disclosure: 'Two recent results disagree; we use the slower one until a new result confirms.'

conditions: Riegel power law used only as a range, never a point; no VDOT table, no VO2max value, no threshold claim.
Changed exponents: STANDARD kLow 1.04, kCentral 1.07, kHigh 1.12 (proposal 1.04/1.06/1.10); MARATHON kLow 1.08, kCentral 1.13, kHigh 1.20 (proposal 1.06/1.10/1.15).

Changed scope: the MARATHON range applies only upward from a half-marathon result (distance ratio at most 2.0) or at the same distance; marathon evidence is never converted to shorter targets or to v(T).
Distance ratio at most 4.3 for STANDARD conversions (kept).
Population: adults, 10K-equivalent central time 27 to 75 minutes; outside, model output is UNAVAILABLE: OUTSIDE_MODEL_POPULATION. A 10K-equivalent of 60 minutes or more adds 0.01 to the margin.
items.rationale: Answer to the question asked: a single power-law range is acceptable for recreational adults up to the half marathon when used as a range with central 1.07 (SRC01 found k = 1.07 well calibrated to the half) and a slow edge reaching the individual-exponent median of 1.12 (SRC02). It is not acceptable for the marathon from shorter races at 1.06-1.10: SRC01 shows a median 10-min and a 5th-centile 36-min underestimate at 1.07, SRC04 finds no equation accurate across abilities, and SRC06 shows recreational marathon intensity spans 79-93% of CS by ability. Slower runners are less consistent (SRC03, SRC05) and are sparse in SRC01 beyond about 7:30/km, hence the 75-min limit and extra margin.
items.disclosure: Every estimate and band names the method: 'estimated with a standard race-time model; individual results vary'.

conditions: Replaced: the band is the athlete's own current 5 km estimate (Q7) turned into a pace band by values.paceRules.racePace, not v(25) to v(15). Without a current 5 km estimate the band is UNAVAILABLE and the session stays effort-only.
items.rationale: Fixed durations of 15-25 min are faster than 5 km race pace for any runner slower than 25 min, which would contradict a 5K-specific session's objective. Race pace from the athlete's own estimate keeps the objective; the effort cue (about 8 of 10) still governs.
items.disclosure: 'Estimated current 5 km race pace; even and controlled, never a sprint; effort governs.'

conditions: Replaced as for FIVE_K_EFFORT: the current 10 km estimate, not v(45) to v(30).
items.rationale: Same objective argument as 5K: for slower runners v(30-45) is faster than their 10 km pace.
items.disclosure: 'Estimated current 10 km race pace; effort governs.'

conditions: Edges by values.paceRules.durationDomain. Named 'controlled threshold effort' only; never LT2, MLSS or critical speed. Requires STANDARD evidence (not marathon-only).
items.rationale: Speeds sustainable for 55-75 min lie below the 20-30-min sustainability of critical speed (SRC07), matching 'you could hold it much longer than the repetition'. Duration anchoring is closer to individual domains than fixed fractions (SRC08, SRC09), but it is still an estimate.
items.disclosure: 'Estimated; comfortably hard and controlled; if it feels harder than 6-7 of 10, slow down.'

conditions: Replaced: the current half-marathon estimate (with its endurance gate, Q7.half), not v(120) to v(80). Rule 7 of the proposal is absorbed: no half estimate, no band.
items.rationale: Race-specific objective; SRC01 supports the model to the half.
items.disclosure: 'Estimated current half-marathon race pace; effort governs.'

conditions: Replaced: the current marathon estimate (Q7.marathon), not v(240) to v(150). No marathon estimate, no band. Withdrawn whenever the race day is a completion.
Not used as a 'moderate continuous' band: the engine has no such family (LATER.RUN.STEADY stays open), so no new session type and no alias.
items.rationale: Marathon pace from short durations is the least reliable conversion (SRC01, SRC06); tying it to the gated marathon estimate keeps the special caution.
items.disclosure: 'Estimated current marathon pace from your half marathon; many runners race the marathon slower than such estimates; effort governs.'

conditions: Fractions kept; edges by values.paceRules.fractionDomain (fast edge with the central exponent and the margin; slow edge with the slowest exponent and twice the margin). The fast edge is a ceiling; slower is always valid; the text never asks to speed up. A P1 observed band replaces it only when slower (Q5.P1).
items.rationale: Fixed fractions do not place individuals in one domain (SRC08, SRC09), so the band cannot be an easy-domain boundary; as a ceiling under the speech cue (SRC21, SRC22) it can only slow a runner, the safe direction, and supports the low-intensity emphasis that benefits recreational runners (SRC24).
items.disclosure: 'Upper limit for easy running, estimated; conversation pace governs; slower is always fine.'

conditions: As EASY. Heat, hills and late-run drift are named; slowing late in the run is expected.
items.rationale: As EASY, slightly slower for duration.
items.disclosure: As EASY.

items.rationale: As EASY; a recovery benefit is never claimed from the band.
items.disclosure: As EASY; never 'this speeds recovery'.

items.rationale: Perceived effort and speech adapt to conditions the model ignores.

items.rationale: Only the slowing direction is safe under uncertain domain placement.
items.disclosure: As Q4.EASY.

conditions: Changed margins: HIGH 0.025, MODERATE 0.04, LOW 0.06 (proposal 0.015/0.03/0.05), plus 0.01 for 10K-equivalent of 60 min or more.

q11.question: Is the existing one-week SYSTEMIC_FATIGUE / LOCAL_FATIGUE adaptation an adequate, safe V1 answer for a screened, sign-free report of ordinary tiredness?
q11.nature: Sporting opinion only; not an approval, not a queue item, no implementation assumed. Whether to expose it is a Founder and Product choice; C.1 as it stands is also safe.
q11.codeRead: fatigue() in r6-adaptation.mjs and fatigueSessions() in r6-composition.mjs: systemic turns the week's remaining QUALITY and RACE_TOUCH runs into easy runs and keeps strength main lifts only with one set fewer and RIR at least 4; local removes only optional accessories of the affected region; the week's gates are held (no ADVANCE or EARNED) by the systemic signal; no window, ladder or chain; the next week is gated by the ordinary weekly review.
q11.rationale: It is a minimum effective change: it removes only the remaining hard stimulus of one week, keeps easy participation, freezes progression for that week and lets executed evidence decide the next, which is lower risk than either continuing hard work while tired or opening a multi-week reduction. No validated marker distinguishes ordinary tiredness from early overreaching or illness (SRC25), so the adaptation is defensible only as a short, self-limiting option behind the screen, with persistence routed to assessment.
conditions: Only after the warning-sign screen with every item actively answered no; an unanswered item is ASK, never this adaptation.
Never when the athlete names illness, infection, injury or pain: those keep the existing clinical route.
An offer the athlete accepts; declining keeps the plan with the C.1 message.

Repetition limit: a second systemic report within 14 days of an applied adaptation, or a third within 42 days, is not reduced again automatically: the athlete gets the C.1 message and the persistent-symptom route (seek a health professional's assessment), owned by G04 and the clinical route, not by this record.
The report never counts as a compatible response and never feeds ADVANCE, EARNED or calibration (Q8).
Local fatigue changes strength accessories only; a running-related local complaint that is pain goes to the screen.

aeReview.level: Policy-level answers; no athlete case was reviewed.
aeReview.q1_currentPlanAdequate: The plan is adequate as an effort-based prescription; it does not meet the Founder's V1 requirement to state pace and current-capacity estimates where evidence allows.
aeReview.q2_materialFact: Declared results, tests and logged sessions with their measurement, date, effort and conditions; nothing inferred from goals, age or easy pace.
aeReview.q3_keepDefensible: KEEP (effort only) stays the fallback for every unavailable case; it is safe but uninformative.
aeReview.q4_changeNecessary: Yes for the guidance layer only; no dose changes.
aeReview.q5_smallestIntervention: An overlay beside the cue, fail-closed, with ceilings for easy running and ranges for everything else.
aeReview.q6_smallerAlternativesInsufficient: Effort-only cannot answer pace or estimate questions; P1 and P2 observations alone give no estimates.
aeReview.q7_priorityAndProgression: Untouched: bands never change gates or doses; a P3 test replaces, never adds, a harder session.
aeReview.q8_evidenceSupportsDose: The model to the half: SUPPORTED_WITH_LIMITS; the marathon from shorter races: not supported (abstained); fractions for easy ceilings and the HR fractions: conventions without individual validity, so ceilings and display only.
aeReview.q9_uncertainty: Exponent spread, measurement error, slow-runner variability, marathon endurance, HR domain placement.
aeReview.q10_askHoldClinical: Unknown eligibility for P3: not eligible. Symptoms in a test or run: the existing screen. Clinical hold: nothing shown.

escalations.what: The catalog rule 'Claim ... finish time' (safety.productMustNot, an approved product decision) needs its formal reading recorded: this record's sporting opinion is that a labelled current-capacity range with 'not a promise' is compatible, and the Founder's request asks for such estimates, but the reading of a product decision is not this role's to publish. Not blocking the sporting values.

Conservative choices with product impact, reversible on new evidence: no marathon estimate from 5 or 10 km results; no 5 km test for novices; P3 only after an executed harder session; bands for slower runners are wide.

Athlete-facing copy for every disclosure; the semantics of measurement sources (OFFICIAL, TRACK, GPS, MANUAL, TREADMILL), condition flags and the 'poor GPS' flag; how RPE and 'tolerated' are collected at intake.
Heart-rate and lab values are health-adjacent data; their handling is outside this role.
Symptoms during a P3 test or any run go to the existing warning-sign screen; the Q11 repetition limit points to the persistent-symptom route owned by G04. This record sets no clinical rule.
